definition: The software layer between the hardware and programs. It turns raw hardware into clean abstractions (processes, files, sockets), shares the hardware out between programs, and stops programs harming each other. In OS theory the term usually means the kernel; in casual use it means a whole distribution.
example: Linux, Windows and macOS are operating systems; Ubuntu is an operating system built on the Linux kernel.

definition: Hiding messy, varied hardware behind a simpler, uniform idea that programs can use without knowing the details. It is one of the three jobs of an operating system, alongside resource management and protection.
example: A program reads a file on an SSD, on a network share or in RAM with the same read call, because the file is an abstraction.

definition: The OS job of sharing limited hardware (CPU time, memory, disk and network bandwidth) between many competing programs, deciding who gets what and for how long.
example: The scheduler deciding which of 400 processes runs on each of 4 cores is resource management.

definition: The OS job of stopping programs from reading or damaging each other's memory, files and devices, and from damaging the kernel. It relies on hardware support: CPU privilege levels and per-process address spaces.
example: A buggy browser tab cannot overwrite your text editor's memory, because each process has its own address space.

definition: Arranging a system so that a bug or crash in one component cannot corrupt or crash the others. Running components in separate processes with separate address spaces is the usual way to get it.
example: In a microkernel a crashed disk driver is just a crashed process that can be restarted; the rest of the system keeps running.

definition: A program that is running: its code plus everything needed to execute it right now, namely an address space, CPU register values, open files and other OS resources, and an identity (a PID). The process is the operating system's central abstraction.
example: Running python3 in three terminals gives one program and three processes, each with its own PID.

definition: A file containing machine instructions and data, sitting passively on disk. A program becomes a process when the OS loads it into memory and starts running it; one program can be running as many processes at once.
example: /usr/bin/python3 is one program file, however many Python processes are running.

definition: A small non-negative integer that a process uses to refer to an open file, pipe, socket or device. It is an index into the process's own table of open files, so the same number means nothing in another process. By convention 0 is standard input, 1 standard output and 2 standard error.
example: open("notes.txt", O_RDONLY) might return 3, and the program then calls read(3, buf, 4096).

definition: An endpoint for communication that a program reads and writes through a file descriptor. Sockets can connect processes on the same machine (Unix domain sockets) or across a network (for example TCP sockets).
example: A web server calls accept on a listening TCP socket to get a new socket for each client connection.

definition: The text interface a shell runs in: originally a physical keyboard-and-screen device, now usually a terminal emulator program. When standard output is a terminal, the C library buffers output line by line.
example: Running ls in a terminal shows its output immediately after each line.

definition: A hardware feature that lets a device such as a disk controller or network card read and write main memory itself, without the CPU copying each byte. Because a DMA-capable device can reach memory directly, the OS must control which memory it may touch.
example: A network card uses DMA to drop incoming packets straight into a ring of buffers in RAM.

definition: A tiny, very fast storage slot inside the CPU that holds a value an instruction is working on, such as a number, an address or the next instruction's location. A process's register values are part of its state and must be saved when it stops running.
example: An x86-64 CPU has 16 general-purpose 64-bit registers such as rax and rdi.

definition: The CPU register that holds the memory address of the next instruction to run. Saving and restoring it is what lets a paused process continue exactly where it stopped. On x86-64 it is called rip.
example: After a context switch the kernel reloads a task's saved instruction pointer so it resumes at the right instruction.

definition: The CPU register that holds the address of the current top of the stack. Each thread has its own stack, so each has its own saved stack pointer. On x86-64 it is called rsp.
example: Calling a function pushes a return address and moves the stack pointer down by 8 bytes on x86-64.

definition: The hardware that connects a computer to a network and sends and receives packets. The kernel's driver for it hands packets to the network stack.
example: When a packet arrives, the NIC writes it into memory and raises an interrupt.

definition: A fixed-size chunk of storage on a disk, typically 512 bytes or 4 KiB, identified by number. Disks only understand reading and writing numbered blocks; the file system builds files and directories on top of them.
example: A 4 KiB file occupies one 4 KiB block on a typical ext4 file system.

definition: The part of the OS that organises disk blocks (or memory, or network storage) into named files and directories, with permissions and metadata. Linux supports many, such as ext4, NFS and tmpfs, behind one interface (the VFS).
example: ext4 is the default file system on many Linux distributions.

definition: The fourth extended file system, a widely used Linux disk file system and the default on many distributions. On Linux it runs inside the kernel.
example: A file read on Linux typically goes from the VFS to ext4 to the block layer to the disk driver.

definition: A protocol, originally from Sun Microsystems in 1984, that lets a machine mount a directory stored on another machine and use it like a local file system. A hung NFS server can leave processes stuck in uninterruptible sleep.
example: A home directory mounted over NFS looks local, but every read crosses the network.

definition: A Linux file system that keeps files in memory (and swap) rather than on disk, so its contents vanish at reboot. /dev/shm, where POSIX shared memory objects live, is a tmpfs.
example: Files written to a tmpfs mount at /tmp never touch the disk.

definition: The part of the kernel that decides which runnable thread runs on each CPU core next, and for how long. It is invoked when a task blocks, wakes, or uses up its time slice.
example: With 400 runnable threads and 4 cores, the scheduler chooses which 4 run at each moment.

definition: Describes a task that has everything it needs to run except a CPU: it is not waiting for I/O, a lock or a timer. Linux shows runnable and running tasks with the same state letter, R.
example: Ten CPU-hungry threads on a 4-core machine means about 6 runnable threads are waiting at any moment.

definition: One independent processing unit inside a CPU chip, able to run its own stream of instructions. A 4-core CPU can run 4 threads truly at the same time (more with SMT).
example: A 4-core laptop runs hundreds of processes by switching each core between them.

definition: What the OS sees as one CPU it can schedule on. Without SMT each core is one logical CPU; with SMT one physical core appears as two (or more) logical CPUs that share its execution units.
example: An 8-core CPU with 2-way SMT shows 16 logical CPUs in top.

definition: A CPU feature that lets one physical core run instructions from two or more threads at once, by sharing its execution units between them. Intel markets it as Hyper-Threading. Each hardware thread appears to the OS as a separate logical CPU.
example: An SMT core can be executing two threads at the same instant, which the textbook "one running thread per CPU" rule has to allow for.

definition: The fixed-size unit in which virtual memory is managed, mapped and protected: 4 KiB on x86-64 by default, with larger huge pages also available. Page tables map each virtual page to a physical frame.
example: A 1 MiB buffer occupies 256 pages of 4 KiB each.

definition: Removing data from a limited fast store to make room for something else: a page pushed out of RAM to disk, or a line pushed out of a CPU cache by another task's data.
example: After another task runs, many of your cache lines have been evicted, so your next accesses are slower.

definition: The part of the Linux kernel that sits between file systems and disk drivers. It queues, merges and orders read and write requests for block devices.
example: Several small writes to neighbouring blocks may be merged by the block layer into one larger disk request.

definition: Moving data between the computer and the outside world: disks, networks, keyboards, screens. I/O is far slower than the CPU, so a process waiting for it usually blocks and lets another run.
example: Reading a file that is not cached means disk I/O, which can take thousands of times longer than reading RAM.

definition: The number the kernel assigns to identify a process. Each process also records its parent's PID (PPID). PIDs are a limited resource: Linux has a maximum (pid_max), so leaked zombies can exhaust them.
example: systemd is PID 1; a shell you start might be PID 2817.

definition: A 16-bit number that identifies which program on a machine a network connection or packet is for. Port numbers are a resource the OS hands out and protects.
example: A web server typically listens on port 443 for HTTPS.

definition: Sharing one resource between many users. In time: taking turns, as processes do on a CPU core. In space: each gets a part, as processes do with RAM.
example: A CPU core time-multiplexes dozens of threads by switching between them many times a second.

definition: A hardware-enforced level of trust that the CPU is running at. Code at the highest level (the kernel) can run every instruction and touch all memory; code at the lowest level (applications) cannot. Every CPU used for general-purpose OSes has at least two.
example: x86 has four rings but Linux uses only ring 0 (kernel) and ring 3 (user).

definition: The x86 name for CPU privilege levels, numbered 0 (most privileged) to 3 (least). Kernels run in ring 0 and applications in ring 3; rings 1 and 2 are rarely used.
example: A syscall moves the CPU from ring 3 to ring 0 and back.

definition: ARM's name for CPU privilege levels. EL0 runs applications, EL1 the OS kernel, EL2 a hypervisor and EL3 secure firmware.
example: An Android app runs at EL0 and enters the Linux kernel at EL1 with the svc instruction.

definition: The family of CPU instruction sets descended from Intel's 8086. x86-64 (also called AMD64) is its 64-bit version, used by most desktop and server PCs.
example: On x86-64 Linux the syscall number goes in the rax register.

definition: A family of CPU instruction sets used in nearly all phones and many laptops and servers. ARM64 (AArch64) is the 64-bit version.
example: On ARM64 Linux the syscall number goes in register x8 and the call is made with svc #0.

definition: A CPU instruction that only runs in kernel mode, such as loading a new page table or disabling interrupts. If user-mode code tries one, the CPU raises an exception instead.
example: Writing the CR3 register on x86 is privileged, so only the kernel can switch address spaces.

definition: The less-privileged CPU mode that ordinary programs run in. Privileged instructions fault, and only memory pages marked user-accessible can be touched.
example: Your code runs at full speed in user mode until it makes a syscall or an interrupt arrives.

definition: The privileged CPU mode the kernel runs in, where every instruction is allowed and kernel memory is accessible. The CPU only enters it through events whose entry addresses the kernel set up in advance.
example: A syscall switches the CPU into kernel mode, and sysret switches it back.

definition: Everything that runs outside the kernel, in user mode: shells, services, libraries and applications. It reaches kernel services only through system calls.
example: bash, systemd and glibc all run in user space.

definition: The memory and privileged mode where the kernel runs. Code there can do anything, so a bug in kernel space can crash or compromise the whole machine.
example: In Linux, file systems and device drivers run in kernel space.

definition: A control or data location on a hardware device that software reads or writes to command it. The kernel normally keeps these out of reach of user programs.
example: A disk driver writes a block number and a memory address into the controller's device registers to start a read.

definition: A signal from hardware that makes the CPU stop what it is doing and jump to a kernel handler, regardless of which program is running. Interrupts are asynchronous: they are unrelated to the current instruction.
example: When a network packet arrives, the NIC raises an interrupt so the kernel can process it.

definition: The code that knows how to control one particular kind of hardware and presents it to the rest of the OS in a standard form. In Linux most drivers run in the kernel; in microkernels they run as user-space processes.
example: An NVMe driver turns the block layer's requests into commands for an NVMe SSD.

definition: A number that identifies a user. On Unix-like systems the UID is the number the kernel uses to identify which user a process runs as; permission checks on files and other resources compare it with the resource's owner. UID 0 is root.
example: A process running as UID 1000 cannot read a file that only UID 0 may read.

definition: The number identifying a group of users. A process has a group ID (and supplementary groups) that the kernel checks against a file's group permissions.
example: Members of a "docker" group may be allowed to use the Docker socket.

definition: The read, write and execute permissions stored with a Unix file for its owner, its group and everyone else, usually written in octal.
example: Mode 0644 means the owner can read and write, everyone else can only read.

definition: One of the separate privileges Linux splits root's power into, such as CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE (bind low ports) or CAP_SYS_ADMIN. A process can hold some capabilities without being fully root.
example: A web server can be given only CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE so it can listen on port 443 without running as root.

definition: The program that reads your commands and starts other programs for you, using fork and exec. It also sets up redirection and pipelines. Bash is the most common on Linux.
example: Typing ls > out.txt makes the shell fork, point the child's standard output at out.txt, then exec ls.

definition: The GNU Bourne Again Shell, the default interactive shell on many Linux systems. It reports a command's exit status in $? and reports a signal death as 128 plus the signal number.
example: After a process is killed by SIGKILL (signal 9), Bash shows status 137.

definition: The init system and service manager used as PID 1 on most Linux distributions. It starts and supervises services, sets their resource limits through cgroups, and reaps orphaned processes.
example: A unit file line MemoryMax=2G tells systemd to cap a service's memory at 2 GB.

definition: A widely used web server and reverse proxy. It handles many connections with a few worker processes, each running an event loop with non-blocking I/O.
example: An nginx worker can serve thousands of connections without a thread per connection.

definition: Google's web browser, built from the open-source Chromium project. It runs tabs and components in separate processes so a fault in one is contained, and uses shared memory to move large buffers between them.
example: Each Chrome tab usually has its own renderer process.

definition: The library that provides C's standard functions (printf, malloc, fopen) and thin wrappers around system calls. On Linux the common ones are glibc and musl.
example: Calling write() in C actually calls the libc wrapper, which executes the syscall instruction.

definition: The GNU project's C library, the standard libc on most Linux distributions. It wraps system calls, implements stdio buffering and the malloc allocator, and converts kernel error returns into -1 plus errno.
example: glibc's posix_spawn uses a clone call that shares memory with the parent until exec.

definition: A small, simple C library for Linux, an alternative to glibc. It is common in small container images such as Alpine Linux.
example: An Alpine-based container links its programs against musl rather than glibc.

definition: The OpenSSL library that implements TLS encryption for programs. Like any library it runs in user space inside the process that uses it.
example: curl and nginx can link libssl to make HTTPS connections.

definition: The layer in the kernel that gives every file system the same interface (open, read, write, close). System calls go to the VFS, which hands them to the right file system, such as ext4 or NFS.
example: cat works on ext4, NFS and tmpfs alike because the VFS presents them all the same way.

definition: The kernel code that implements network protocols such as IP, TCP and UDP, between sockets above and network drivers below.
example: Data written to a TCP socket passes down the network stack, gets split into segments and goes out through the NIC driver.

definition: The C library function that formats text and writes it to standard output. It writes into a user-space stdio buffer, so it only makes a write syscall when that buffer is flushed.
example: A thousand printf calls to a file may produce a single write syscall.

definition: The buffered input/output part of the C library (printf, fopen, fflush). It collects output in a user-space buffer and only makes a write syscall when the buffer is flushed, to save syscalls.
example: fflush(stdout) forces stdio to write out whatever it has buffered.

definition: A complete operating system built around the Linux kernel, bundling it with a C library, shell, utilities, an init system and usually a package manager. Ubuntu, Debian and Fedora are distributions.
example: Ubuntu is a distribution; Linux itself is only its kernel.

definition: A popular Linux distribution published by Canonical, based on Debian.
example: An Ubuntu server runs the Linux kernel with systemd as PID 1.

definition: The open-source, monolithic, Unix-like kernel started by Linus Torvalds in 1991. Strictly it is only the kernel; full operating systems built on it are called distributions.
example: Android and most web servers run on the Linux kernel.

definition: A kernel design where all core OS services (scheduler, memory manager, file systems, network stack and device drivers) run together in kernel space as one program. It is fast, because components call each other directly, but a bug in any part has full privilege.
example: Linux and FreeBSD are monolithic kernels.

definition: A kernel design that keeps only the minimum in kernel space (address spaces, threads, scheduling and IPC) and runs drivers, file systems and network stacks as ordinary user-space processes. It isolates faults but pays for extra IPC.
example: seL4, QNX and MINIX 3 are microkernels.

definition: A kernel that starts from a microkernel-style design but moves performance-critical services (file systems, drivers) back into kernel space. Critics say this makes it behave much like a monolithic kernel.
example: Windows NT and Apple's XNU are usually called hybrid kernels.

definition: An open-source Unix-like operating system descended from BSD Unix, with a monolithic kernel. It is used in servers, network appliances and as a base for other systems.
example: Parts of macOS's BSD layer come from FreeBSD.

definition: The operating system created at Bell Labs around 1970, and the family of systems that copy its design: processes created by fork and exec, everything as files, and small tools joined by pipes. Linux, BSD and macOS are Unix-like.
example: Unix shells build pipelines like ls | wc -l from pipe, fork and exec.

definition: A standard interface for fast solid-state drives attached over PCI Express, designed for many parallel request queues.
example: A modern laptop SSD is usually an NVMe drive.

definition: A storage device that keeps data in flash memory chips, with no moving parts. It is much faster than a spinning hard disk but still far slower than RAM.
example: Reading 4 KiB from an SSD typically takes tens of microseconds.

definition: What happens when the kernel detects an error it cannot safely recover from: it stops the machine (or reboots it), because continuing could corrupt data.
example: A bad driver that corrupts kernel memory can cause a kernel panic.

definition: A Linux kernel error report for a serious but not always fatal fault, such as a bad pointer dereference in kernel code. The kernel logs a backtrace and kills the offending task; the system may keep running but is no longer trustworthy.
example: A crash inside a loaded module produces an oops in the kernel log.

definition: A piece of kernel code, usually a driver, stored as a separate file (.ko on Linux) and loaded into the running kernel on demand. Once loaded it runs in kernel mode with full privilege and no isolation.
example: modprobe e1000e loads the Intel network driver module without a reboot.

definition: Linux commands for kernel modules: modprobe loads a module with its dependencies, insmod loads one file directly, lsmod lists loaded modules and rmmod removes one.
example: lsmod | grep ext4 shows whether ext4 is loaded as a module.

definition: A Linux facility for running small programs inside the kernel, for example for tracing, networking or security. Each program is checked by an in-kernel verifier before it runs, to limit what it can do.
example: A tracing tool can attach an eBPF program to every openat syscall to log which files are opened.

definition: The kernel-provided ways for separate processes to exchange data and events, such as pipes, signals, shared memory, message queues and sockets. In a microkernel, IPC is also how applications reach drivers and file systems.
example: A shell pipeline uses a pipe, one kind of IPC, to connect ls to wc.

definition: In a microkernel system, an ordinary user-space process that provides an OS service such as a file system, network stack or driver. Applications send it requests by IPC.
example: On QNX the file system runs as a server process; if it crashes it can be restarted.

definition: A family of small, fast microkernels descended from Jochen Liedtke's L4 (1993), which showed that IPC could be made far cheaper than in earlier microkernels such as Mach.
example: seL4 is a member of the L4 family.

definition: A microkernel in the L4 family with machine-checked mathematical proofs that its code matches its specification, for particular architectures and configurations and under stated assumptions.
example: seL4 is used in some high-assurance and defence systems because of its proofs.

definition: Using mathematical proof, checked by a computer, to show that a piece of software behaves exactly as its specification says. It is only practical for small code bases, which is one reason small kernels appeal.
example: seL4's original functional-correctness proof (2009) covered about 8,700 lines of C, and the kernel is usually described as roughly 10,000 lines.

definition: A commercial real-time operating system built on a microkernel, now owned by BlackBerry. Drivers and services run as separate user-space processes, and it is widely used in cars and industrial systems.
example: Many car infotainment systems run QNX.

definition: A small Unix-like teaching operating system written by Andrew Tanenbaum. MINIX 3 is a microkernel design aimed at reliability, with drivers that can be restarted after crashes.
example: Linus Torvalds used MINIX before writing Linux.

definition: An early microkernel developed at Carnegie Mellon University from 1985. It was notoriously slow because of IPC costs, but lives on inside Apple's XNU kernel.
example: macOS's kernel combines Mach with a BSD layer.

definition: A 1992 Usenet argument in which Andrew Tanenbaum, author of MINIX, posted that "Linux is obsolete" because it was monolithic, and Linus Torvalds defended the monolithic design on performance and simplicity grounds.
example: The debate is still cited when microkernels and monolithic kernels are compared.

definition: The kernel family behind all modern versions of Windows, first released in 1993. It is usually described as a hybrid kernel: a layered kernel and "executive" with file systems, the network stack and most drivers running in kernel mode.
example: Windows 11 runs on the NT kernel.

definition: The kernel of macOS and iOS ("X is Not Unix"). It combines the Mach microkernel, a BSD layer and the IOKit driver framework, all running in kernel space, so it is usually called a hybrid kernel.
example: A macOS system call enters the XNU kernel.

definition: The Berkeley Software Distribution, a version of Unix from the University of California, Berkeley, and the family of systems descended from it (FreeBSD, OpenBSD, NetBSD). XNU includes a BSD layer for POSIX processes, networking and the VFS.
example: macOS's Unix commands and sockets come largely from BSD.

definition: Apple's object-oriented framework for writing device drivers in the XNU kernel.
example: A macOS USB driver traditionally ran in the kernel as an IOKit extension.

definition: Apple's desktop and laptop operating system, built on the XNU kernel.
example: A Mac runs macOS; its kernel is XNU.

definition: Apple's operating system for the iPhone, built on the same XNU kernel as macOS.
example: An iPhone app runs in user space on top of XNU.

definition: Apple's framework, introduced with macOS 10.15 in 2019, for writing certain device drivers as user-space programs instead of kernel extensions, so a driver crash cannot take down the kernel.
example: A USB device driver written with DriverKit runs as a separate process.

definition: Microsoft's framework for writing some Windows drivers to run in user mode rather than kernel mode, so a driver bug cannot crash the whole system.
example: Many USB device drivers on Windows can be written with UMDF.

definition: The main file system of Windows NT and its successors. It runs in kernel mode.
example: A Windows system drive is normally formatted as NTFS.

definition: The Linux user-space device manager. When the kernel reports a device, udev creates its entry under /dev, gives it a stable name and runs any configured rules.
example: udev is why a USB disk can always appear under the same /dev/disk/by-id name.

definition: A Linux user-space service that configures network interfaces (Wi-Fi, Ethernet, VPNs). It decides policy, such as which network to join, using kernel networking mechanisms.
example: Clicking a Wi-Fi network on a Linux desktop asks NetworkManager to connect.

definition: A design principle: the kernel provides mechanisms (what can be done, such as preempting a thread or capping a group's memory), while separate code, often in user space, sets policy (what should be done, such as which service gets 2 GB). Keeping them apart lets policy change without rewriting mechanism.
example: The kernel provides cgroups (mechanism); systemd unit files decide each service's limits (policy).

definition: The length of time the scheduler lets a thread run before it may be preempted so another can have a turn. Typical values are a few milliseconds.
example: When a CPU-bound thread's time slice runs out, the timer interrupt lets the kernel switch to another thread.

definition: A thread the kernel itself knows about and schedules. It can mean a thread that runs only kernel code (background work such as flushing dirty pages) or, in threading models, the kernel-scheduled thread under a user-level thread.
example: In ps, kernel threads such as kworker appear in square brackets.

definition: An event raised by the CPU because of the instruction it is running, such as a page fault or divide by zero, which transfers control to a kernel handler. Some are fixable (the kernel maps a page and retries); others end the process with a signal.
example: Dividing an integer by zero on x86 raises a divide-error exception, which Linux turns into SIGFPE.

definition: The kernel taking the CPU away from a task that could have kept running, usually because its time slice ran out or a higher-priority task woke up. It is an involuntary context switch.
example: A thread stuck in while (1); is preempted when the timer interrupt fires, so other tasks still get a turn.

definition: A regular interrupt from a hardware timer that hands control back to the kernel even if the running program never makes a syscall. It is what lets the scheduler preempt a task that would otherwise run forever.
example: Without the timer interrupt, a program in an infinite loop could keep a core forever.

definition: Imitating a CPU or device in software, interpreting each instruction instead of running it directly on the hardware. It is much slower than direct execution.
example: Running ARM code on an x86 PC with QEMU in full emulation mode is many times slower than native.

definition: A Linux kernel feature that groups processes and accounts for or caps their CPU, memory and I/O use. Container runtimes and systemd use it to apply resource limits.
example: A container limited to 512 MB of memory is enforced by its cgroup.

definition: A configuration file describing a service (or other unit) for systemd: what to run, when, and with which limits, such as MemoryMax=2G.
example: Editing a service's unit file to set MemoryMax=2G caps its memory without touching the kernel.

definition: A Unix setting from −20 (highest priority) to 19 (lowest) that tells the scheduler how favourably to treat a process relative to others.
example: Running a backup with nice -n 19 makes it yield the CPU to interactive work.

definition: A mechanism (RFC 4862) in which a host builds its own IPv6 address from the prefix that routers announce in Router Advertisement messages, without a DHCP server. On Linux the kernel can do it itself.
example: A Linux laptop can get a global IPv6 address from SLAAC as soon as a router advertises a prefix.

definition: An operating system designed to respond within guaranteed time limits, as needed in controllers, medical devices and cars.
example: QNX is an RTOS used in safety-related automotive systems.

definition: Linux running on a dedicated device such as a router, TV or industrial controller, rather than a general-purpose computer.
example: Many home Wi-Fi routers run embedded Linux.

definition: A hardware or software timer that resets or restarts something if it is not "fed" regularly. It detects hangs but cannot prevent memory corruption.
example: If a driver stops responding for 5 seconds, a watchdog can reset the device.

definition: A pointer holding a bad address, so writing through it corrupts whatever memory happens to be there. In kernel space that can be any part of the kernel.
example: A driver bug that writes through a freed pointer is a wild write.

definition: All the code that must be correct for a system's security or safety to hold. The smaller it is, the less there is to review, test or certify.
example: Moving third-party drivers out of the kernel shrinks the trusted computing base.

definition: Formal evidence, reviewed against a standard, that a system such as a medical or automotive device is acceptably safe. A safety case is the structured argument and evidence for it.
example: Medical device software is assessed against standards such as IEC 62304.

definition: The error screen Windows shows when its kernel hits a fatal error, the Windows equivalent of a kernel panic.
example: A buggy kernel-mode driver can blue-screen Windows.

definition: The IEEE standard that defines a common Unix-like operating system interface: system calls such as fork and read, signals, threads and shell behaviour. Code written to POSIX is portable between Linux, BSD and macOS.
example: POSIX requires PIPE_BUF to be at least 512 bytes.

definition: The first user-space process, started by the kernel at boot, which becomes the ancestor of every other process. It adopts orphans and must reap them, and it is protected from signals it has no handler for. On most Linux systems it is systemd.
example: In a container, the application itself is often PID 1 inside its PID namespace.

definition: A Linux framework that lets a small kernel stub expose a device's memory and interrupts to a user-space driver, which does the rest of the work.
example: An industrial I/O card can be driven from a user-space program through UIO.

definition: A command-line tool and library for transferring data with URLs, most often over HTTP.
example: curl https://example.com fetches a web page.

definition: The device driver for a graphics card. GPU drivers are large and complex, so on a monolithic kernel a bug in one can corrupt unrelated kernel memory.
example: A faulty GPU driver can cause a kernel panic on Linux.

definition: Starting a computer: firmware loads the kernel, the kernel sets up hardware and its own tables (including syscall entry points), then starts PID 1.
example: Linux registers its syscall entry address in an MSR during boot.

definition: The file containing the compiled kernel that the boot loader loads into memory. Drivers built as modules live in separate files and are not part of it.
example: On many distributions the kernel image is /boot/vmlinuz.

definition: The screen-based system in a car that handles navigation, media and phone connections. Many run QNX, Linux or Android.
example: A car's touchscreen for maps and music is its infotainment system.

definition: A synchronous transfer of control into more privileged code (the kernel, or a hypervisor) caused by the instruction being run. It may be deliberate, as when a program executes syscall (x86-64) or svc (ARM) to make a system call, or caused by a fault or a privileged instruction the CPU will not run at the current level. Some books reserve "trap" for the deliberate kind.
example: Calling read() ends with a trap into the kernel via the syscall instruction; in a virtual machine, a privileged instruction in the guest traps to the hypervisor.

definition: A kind of CPU exception caused by the current instruction that the kernel may be able to fix, after which the instruction is re-run. If it cannot be fixed, the process usually gets a signal such as SIGSEGV.
example: A page fault on a lazily allocated page is fixed by the kernel mapping the page and retrying the instruction.

definition: Happening because of the instruction the CPU is currently running, at a predictable point. Traps and exceptions are synchronous; device interrupts are not.
example: A divide-by-zero is synchronous: it always happens on the divide instruction.

definition: Happening independently of what the program is currently doing, at an unpredictable moment. Hardware interrupts and signals are asynchronous.
example: A network packet can arrive in the middle of any instruction of any program, so its interrupt is asynchronous.

definition: The technique of running a program directly on the CPU at full speed, while hardware privilege levels limit what it can do and the timer interrupt guarantees the kernel regains control.
example: Your code runs natively in user mode, but a privileged instruction faults and a timer interrupt hands control back to the kernel.

definition: The place where execution starts (or, more loosely, where requests enter a system). For the kernel, the fixed addresses it registers at boot for syscalls, exceptions and interrupts, the only places user code can enter. For a program, the first instruction exec jumps to.
example: Linux stores the address of entry_SYSCALL_64 in an MSR, so every syscall instruction lands there.

definition: The x86-64 instruction that performs a system call: it switches to ring 0 and jumps to the address the kernel stored in the MSR_LSTAR register, saving the return address in rcx and the flags in r11.
example: glibc's write() puts 1 in rax and then executes the syscall instruction.

definition: The x86-64 instruction that returns from a system call to user mode, restoring the instruction pointer from rcx and the flags from r11.
example: After a syscall finishes, Linux often returns to ring 3 with sysret.

definition: The x86 "interrupt return" instruction, which returns from an interrupt or exception handler, restoring the saved instruction pointer, flags and stack. Linux also uses it on some syscall return paths.
example: If sysret cannot be used safely, Linux returns from a syscall with iret.

definition: The ARM "supervisor call" instruction that a program uses to make a system call, moving from EL0 to EL1.
example: On ARM64 Linux, write is called by putting 64 in x8 and executing svc #0.

definition: The error when a program accesses memory it is not allowed to, such as an unmapped address or a write to read-only memory. On Unix the kernel sends the process SIGSEGV, whose default action kills it with a core dump.
example: Dereferencing a null pointer on Linux normally causes a segfault.

definition: The signal (number 11 on Linux) sent for an invalid memory access. Its default action terminates the process and writes a core dump.
example: A program killed by SIGSEGV shows exit status 139 in Bash (128 + 11).

definition: Delaying the real work of giving a process memory until it first touches it. The kernel only promises address space; the first access page-faults and the kernel then supplies a physical page.
example: malloc of 1 GiB returns immediately; physical RAM is used only for the pages actually written.

definition: Named 64-bit general-purpose registers of x86-64. In the Linux syscall convention rax holds the syscall number and the return value, and rdi, rsi, rdx, r10, r8 and r9 hold up to six arguments; the syscall instruction overwrites rcx and r11.
example: write(1, "hi\n", 3) puts 1 in rax, 1 in rdi, the buffer address in rsi and 3 in rdx.

definition: The ARM64 general-purpose register that holds the syscall number in the Linux ARM64 calling convention.
example: On ARM64 Linux, getpid is called with 172 in x8.

definition: The x86-64 register holding status and control flags, such as whether the last result was zero and whether interrupts are enabled. The syscall instruction saves it in r11.
example: After a comparison, a conditional jump reads the zero flag in RFLAGS.

definition: A special x86 control register, readable and writable only in kernel mode, used to configure CPU features. MSR_LSTAR holds the address the syscall instruction jumps to.
example: At boot Linux writes the address of its syscall entry code into MSR_LSTAR.

definition: The agreed rules for how a function receives its arguments and returns a result: which registers or stack slots are used and which registers must be preserved.
example: In the x86-64 System V C convention the fourth argument goes in rcx, but in the Linux syscall convention it goes in r10.

definition: The machine-level contract between compiled pieces of software: calling conventions, register use, data layout and system call numbers. Programs compiled against an ABI keep working without recompiling.
example: The Linux x86-64 syscall ABI fixes write as syscall number 1.

definition: Linux kernel functions that copy data between user memory and kernel memory, checking that the user address really belongs to user space and handling faults safely. The kernel never trusts a user pointer directly.
example: write() uses copy_from_user to fetch the bytes from the caller's buffer.

definition: The C variable (per thread) that holds the error code after a library or system call reports failure, usually by returning -1. It is only meaningful straight after a call that failed.
example: If open() returns -1 and errno is 2 (ENOENT), the file does not exist.

definition: The error code (9 on Linux) meaning "bad file descriptor": the fd is not open, or not open for the requested operation.
example: Writing to an fd that was already closed fails with EBADF.

definition: The error code (4 on Linux) meaning a blocking call was interrupted by a signal handler before it completed. Robust code retries the call.
example: A read() waiting on an empty pipe returns -1 with errno EINTR if a handler runs without SA_RESTART.

definition: The error code (11 on Linux) meaning "try again": the operation would block on a non-blocking descriptor, or a resource such as the process limit is temporarily exhausted.
example: fork() fails with EAGAIN when the user has reached their process limit.

definition: The error code (32 on Linux) returned by a write to a pipe or socket whose reading end has been closed, when SIGPIPE is ignored or blocked.
example: A server that ignores SIGPIPE sees write() fail with EPIPE when a client disconnects.

definition: The error code (10 on Linux) returned by wait or waitpid when the calling process has no child it could wait for.
example: A reaping loop that calls waitpid after every child is gone gets -1 with ECHILD.

definition: The error code (22 on Linux) meaning an argument to a call was invalid.
example: Passing an unknown flag to a syscall typically fails with EINVAL.

definition: A Linux tool that runs a program and prints every system call it makes, with arguments and results. -c prints a summary table and -f follows child processes.
example: strace -e trace=write ./prog shows each write syscall the program makes.

definition: The three file descriptors every Unix process starts with: 0 standard input, 1 standard output and 2 standard error. Shells redirect them to files and pipes.
example: ls > out.txt makes fd 1 (stdout) of ls refer to out.txt.

definition: A stdio mode where output is held in a buffer and written out at each newline. The C library uses it when standard output is a terminal.
example: printf("a\n") on a terminal appears immediately because the newline flushes the line buffer.

definition: A stdio mode where output is held until the buffer fills (typically 4 KiB or more) or is explicitly flushed. The C library uses it when standard output is a file or pipe.
example: printf to a redirected file may not reach the file until the program exits.

definition: A region of memory that holds data temporarily on its way somewhere, so it can be moved in larger, fewer pieces or so a fast producer and slow consumer can work at different speeds.
example: Copying a file with a 64 KiB buffer moves 64 KiB per read and write call.

definition: Writing out data that has been held in a buffer, or (for a TLB or cache) discarding the stored entries.
example: exit() flushes stdio buffers; _exit() does not.

definition: A Linux defence against Meltdown, added in 2018, that gives user mode a page table containing almost no kernel memory and switches to the full kernel page table on every kernel entry and exit. It makes syscalls more expensive, especially without PCID.
example: After KPTI was enabled, syscall-heavy workloads on affected Intel CPUs slowed noticeably.

definition: A CPU vulnerability disclosed in January 2018 that let user-mode code read kernel memory through speculative execution on many Intel (and some other) processors. KPTI is the main software fix.
example: Meltdown is why Linux started unmapping most of the kernel while user code runs.

definition: A family of CPU vulnerabilities, disclosed in 2018, that trick speculative execution into leaking data. The mitigations add barriers and other work to kernel entry and exit.
example: Spectre mitigations are one reason a syscall costs more on some CPUs than it once did.

definition: The layers of small, fast memory between the CPU and RAM. L1 is smallest and fastest (tens of KiB per core), L2 larger, and L3 the largest (several to tens of MiB, often shared between cores). A miss in one level falls through to the next, then to RAM.
example: Refilling a line from L3 takes tens of nanoseconds; from RAM, closer to a hundred.

definition: The part of a CPU that guesses which way a conditional jump will go so it can keep fetching instructions. It learns from history, so kernel code running in between can disturb its predictions for user code.
example: A loop branch that is almost always taken is predicted correctly nearly every time.

definition: Combining many small operations into fewer, larger ones so fixed per-operation costs, such as a syscall's entry and exit, are paid less often.
example: Sending 32 UDP packets with one sendmmsg call instead of 32 sendto calls is batching.

definition: System calls that read into, or write from, several separate buffers in one call.
example: A web server can send headers and body from two buffers with one writev.

definition: A Linux system call that sends several messages (for example UDP packets) on a socket in one call.
example: A DNS server can reply to many queries with one sendmmsg.

definition: Linux system calls that move data between two file descriptors inside the kernel, without copying it out to a user-space buffer and back.
example: A static file server can use sendfile to send a file straight from the page cache to a socket.

definition: A Linux interface, added in kernel 5.1 (2019), in which a program puts I/O requests into a ring buffer shared with the kernel and collects completions from another, submitting many requests with one syscall or, with kernel polling, none.
example: A database can keep hundreds of reads in flight with io_uring while making few syscalls.

definition: A ring buffer (circular buffer) placed in memory that two parties can both see, here a program and the kernel. A ring buffer is a fixed-size queue whose read and write positions wrap round from the last slot to the first; sharing it lets requests and results pass between program and kernel without a syscall per item.
example: io_uring uses one shared ring for submissions and another for completions.

definition: A small shared library the Linux kernel maps into every process. It runs a few read-only calls, such as clock_gettime, in user mode by reading a data page the kernel keeps updated, so they need no syscall.
example: On x86-64, clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC) normally completes inside the vDSO without entering the kernel.

definition: The POSIX call that reads a clock, such as CLOCK_MONOTONIC (time that never jumps backwards). gettimeofday is an older equivalent. On Linux both are usually served by the vDSO.
example: Profilers call clock_gettime millions of times a second to time code.

definition: An x86 CPU register that counts up at a steady rate and can be read from user mode. The vDSO combines it with kernel-supplied data to compute the current time without a syscall.
example: The rdtsc instruction reads the timestamp counter.

definition: The hardware counter the Linux kernel uses for timekeeping, such as the TSC. If it cannot be read from user mode, the vDSO falls back to a real syscall.
example: Some virtual machines use a clock source the vDSO cannot read, making clock_gettime much slower.

definition: A virtual file system on Linux that exposes kernel information about each process (/proc/<pid>/status, maps, fd) and the system as readable files. Nothing in it is stored on disk.
example: cat /proc/self/maps lists every memory region of the cat process itself.

definition: A virtual file system on Linux that exposes devices, drivers and kernel settings as files.
example: Reading /sys/devices/system/clocksource/clocksource0/current_clocksource shows the active clock source.

definition: A sigaction flag asking the kernel to restart many blocking system calls automatically after a signal handler runs, instead of failing them with EINTR.
example: With SA_RESTART set, a read on a pipe resumes after the handler and the caller never sees EINTR.

definition: A function a process registers to run when a particular signal arrives. It can run between any two instructions of the program, so it may only call async-signal-safe functions.
example: A SIGTERM handler that sets a "stop" flag lets a server shut down cleanly.

definition: The condition when there is no more data to read. On Unix read() signals it by returning 0; on a pipe that happens only when every write end is closed.
example: Reading a 10-byte file with a 4 KiB buffer returns 10, then 0 (EOF).

definition: A read or write that moves fewer bytes than requested. It is normal, not an error, especially on pipes and sockets, so robust code loops until it has everything.
example: read(fd, buf, 65536) on a socket may return just 1,200 bytes.

definition: The Unix system call that returns a file's metadata: size, owner, permissions and timestamps.
example: ls -l calls stat (or a variant) on every file it lists.

definition: Code that runs extremely often, so small per-iteration costs such as a syscall dominate total time.
example: A per-request stat() call sits on a busy server's hot path.

definition: A measurement of where a program spends its time, made by a tool called a profiler, such as perf.
example: A profile showing 30 % of time in clock_gettime hints that the vDSO fast path is not being used.

definition: Placing the kernel at a random address at each boot, so attackers cannot rely on knowing where kernel code and data are.
example: With KASLR the kernel's base address differs between reboots.

definition: The x86 table, set up by the kernel, that lists the handler address for each interrupt and exception number. The CPU consults it on every interrupt.
example: When the timer fires, the CPU looks up the timer's vector in the IDT and jumps to the kernel handler.

definition: A memory page whose page-table entry marks it as accessible only in kernel mode. Any user-mode access to it faults.
example: Kernel code pages are supervisor-only, so a user program cannot jump into them.

definition: The all-powerful Unix user account, UID 0, which passes most permission checks. Root processes still run in user mode; root is a kernel permission check, not a CPU privilege level.
example: Running a program as root lets it read any file, but it still enters the kernel through syscalls.

definition: A change of CPU privilege level, such as user to kernel on a syscall and back again, while the same task keeps running. It is cheaper than a context switch, which changes which task runs.
example: getpid() causes two mode switches and no context switch.

definition: The POSIX system call for installing a signal handler and setting its flags (such as SA_RESTART) and mask.
example: sigaction(SIGTERM, &sa, NULL) installs the handler stored in sa.

definition: A C library function that prints a message followed by the text for the current errno.
example: perror("write") prints "write: Bad file descriptor" after an EBADF failure.

definition: Adding structure to a byte stream so the receiver can tell where each message ends, for example a length prefix or a newline delimiter.
example: Prefixing each message with a 4-byte length lets the reader know exactly how many bytes to collect.

definition: One unit of data carried by TCP inside an IP packet, typically up to about 1,460 bytes on Ethernet. A large write may arrive as several segments.
example: A 65,536-byte message usually crosses the network as dozens of TCP segments.

definition: The kernel memory where data that has arrived on a socket waits until the program reads it.
example: read() on a socket returns whatever is in its receive buffer right now, up to the size requested.

definition: The system call that returns the calling process's PID. On x86-64 Linux it is syscall number 39 and is a real syscall, not served by the vDSO.
example: getpid() is a common example of a syscall that only causes a mode switch.

definition: The system calls that open a file and return a new file descriptor. Flags such as O_RDONLY, O_WRONLY, O_RDWR, O_CREAT and O_TRUNC choose the access mode and behaviour.
example: open("out.txt", O_WRONLY | O_CREAT | O_TRUNC, 0644) creates or empties out.txt for writing.

definition: The kernel's table mapping each syscall number to the function that implements it. The number in rax picks the entry.
example: On x86-64 Linux, number 1 dispatches to the write implementation.

definition: The US chip maker that created the x86 architecture. Its manuals call all CPU entry events "interrupts and exceptions".
example: Intel's Software Developer's Manual documents the syscall instruction.

definition: The kernel's record of a process: its state, saved registers, memory map, open files, credentials, scheduling and signal information. It holds everything needed to pause the process and resume it later.
example: In Linux the PCB is struct task_struct.

definition: The Linux kernel structure that describes one task (a thread). It plays the role of the textbook process control block; threads of one process point to shared memory and file-table structures.
example: Each Linux thread has its own task_struct, but threads of one process share the same mm.

definition: The Linux kernel's word for a schedulable thread of execution, described by a task_struct. A single-threaded process is one task; a multithreaded process is several.
example: A process with 8 threads is 8 tasks to the Linux scheduler.

definition: The CPU hardware that translates virtual addresses to physical addresses on every memory access, using the current page tables, and enforces page permissions.
example: When a process loads from address 0x400000, the MMU finds which physical frame that is.

definition: The range of memory addresses a process can use, mapped by its own page tables onto physical memory. Each process has its own, so the same address in two processes can hold different data.
example: Two processes can both use address 0x400000 and see completely different contents.

definition: An address as a program sees it. The MMU translates it to a physical address using page tables.
example: A pointer printed by a C program is a virtual address.

definition: The actual RAM chips and the addresses that identify locations in them. Programs never see these directly; the MMU maps virtual addresses onto them.
example: Two processes' virtual pages at the same address map to different physical pages.

definition: A page-sized slot of physical memory that a virtual page can be mapped to.
example: After a copy-on-write fault the child's page points to a new physical frame.

definition: The x86-64 page-table scheme that translates 48-bit virtual addresses through four levels of tables, giving 256 TiB of virtual space split between user and kernel. Five-level paging adds a level for 57-bit addresses.
example: With four-level paging, Linux user space spans 128 TiB.

definition: An x86-64 virtual address that does not follow the rule that its unused top bits copy the highest used bit. Using one faults, so there is a huge unusable gap between the user half and the kernel half.
example: With 48-bit addresses, 0x0000800000000000 is non-canonical.

definition: The region of a process's address space holding its machine code. It is read-only and executable, and can be shared between processes running the same program.
example: Three python3 processes share one copy of the interpreter's text pages in RAM.

definition: The read-only data region of a program: string literals and const globals. Writing to it faults on conventional Linux builds.
example: The string "hi" in const char *s = "hi" lives in rodata.

definition: The region holding global and static variables that have a non-zero initial value. Their values are stored in the executable file.
example: int g_init = 42; at file scope lives in the data segment.

definition: The region holding global and static variables that start at zero or have no initialiser. The executable records only its size; the kernel supplies zero-filled pages at load time, so it costs nothing on disk.
example: static char buf[100000000]; adds 100 MB of BSS but almost nothing to the file size.

definition: The region of a process's memory used for dynamic allocation with malloc. Memory there lives until it is freed. It grows upwards with the brk syscall; large allocations may instead get their own mmap.
example: malloc(16) returns 16 bytes of heap memory.

definition: The region holding each function call's local variables and return address, growing downwards as functions are called and shrinking as they return. Each thread has its own; on Linux the main thread's is usually limited to 8 MiB.
example: Deep recursion that uses more than the stack limit crashes with SIGSEGV.

definition: The block of stack space one function call uses: its local variables, saved registers and return address.
example: A recursive function using 1 KiB per frame can nest about 8,192 deep in an 8 MiB stack.

definition: The system call that maps a file or anonymous memory into a process's address space, and the region of the address space where such mappings (shared libraries, big allocations, mapped files) live. munmap removes a mapping.
example: glibc serves a 1 MiB malloc with its own mmap, and free returns it with munmap.

definition: A library of code (a .so file on Linux) loaded at run time and mapped into many processes, which share one copy of its code in RAM.
example: libc.so.6 is mapped into almost every process on a glibc system.

definition: The system call that moves the end of a process's heap (the program break) up or down, growing or shrinking the classic heap region.
example: glibc's malloc calls brk to extend the heap when its free lists run out.

definition: The C library function that allocates memory dynamically and returns a pointer to it; free releases it. glibc serves small requests from heap arenas and large ones from separate mmap mappings.
example: int *h = malloc(16); asks for 16 bytes of heap memory.

definition: The allocation size above which glibc's malloc uses a separate mmap instead of the heap. It starts at 128 KiB and normally adjusts itself dynamically.
example: A 1 MiB malloc is above the default threshold, so it gets its own mapping.

definition: A pool of memory that an allocator carves allocations from. glibc uses several arenas so threads can allocate without all contending for one lock.
example: Freed small blocks go back into their arena for reuse rather than back to the kernel.

definition: An allocator's list of freed blocks available for reuse by later allocations.
example: After free(p), the block is placed on a free list and may be returned by the next malloc of a similar size.

definition: The library code, such as glibc's malloc, that hands out and takes back blocks of memory within a process, asking the kernel for more address space when needed.
example: jemalloc and glibc malloc are different allocators with different fragmentation behaviour.

definition: Unmapped memory deliberately left next to a stack so that overrunning the stack faults immediately instead of silently corrupting other memory.
example: Recursion past the stack limit touches the guard region and the process gets SIGSEGV.

definition: A cap on how much of a resource something may use. On Unix-like systems an rlimit is a per-process cap the kernel enforces, such as stack size (RLIMIT_STACK) or the number of processes a user may have (RLIMIT_NPROC). Children inherit them.
example: ulimit -s shows the stack limit, often 8192 (KiB).

definition: A shell built-in that shows or sets the shell's resource limits, which programs it starts inherit.
example: ulimit -s 16384 raises the stack limit to 16 MiB for programs started from that shell.

definition: Using a pointer whose value is null (address 0) to read or write memory. In C it is undefined behaviour; on ordinary Linux systems page zero is unmapped, so it usually faults.
example: *(int *)0 = 1; normally crashes with SIGSEGV on Linux.

definition: In C and C++, an operation the language standard places no requirements on, such as modifying a string literal. The compiler and machine may then do anything, including appearing to work.
example: Writing to a string literal is undefined behaviour; on Linux it commonly faults.

definition: Loading the stack, heap, libraries and (for PIE binaries) the program at random addresses each run, so an attacker cannot predict where code and data are.
example: With ASLR, a library's address differs from run to run; /proc/sys/kernel/randomize_va_space = 2 means full randomisation on Linux.

definition: An executable compiled so it can run at any address, which lets ASLR move the main program as well as its libraries. Modern distributions build PIE by default.
example: A non-PIE binary's code always loads at the same address, which helps attackers.

definition: Text written in quotes in source code, such as "hello". In C it is stored in read-only memory on conventional builds, and modifying it is undefined behaviour.
example: char *s = "hello"; points s at a string literal in rodata.

definition: A variable defined outside any function, which exists for the whole run of the program. It lives in the data or BSS segment.
example: int a = 5; at file scope is a global in the data segment.

definition: A C variable declared static, which, like a global, exists for the whole run and lives in data or BSS rather than on the stack.
example: static int b; inside a file is zero-initialised and lives in BSS.

definition: A variable declared inside a function. It normally lives on the stack and disappears when the function returns.
example: int c = 1; inside f() is a local on the stack.

definition: A variable that holds a memory address. In C the pointer itself and the memory it points to can live in different regions.
example: In int *d = malloc(4);, d is on the stack while *d is on the heap.

definition: A C keyword marking data as not to be modified through that name. const globals usually live in the read-only rodata section.
example: Writing through a const char * is rejected by the compiler without a cast.

definition: How much of a process's memory is currently in physical RAM, as opposed to merely reserved or swapped out. Linux shows it as VmRSS in /proc/<pid>/status.
example: A process that reserved 2 GB but touched only 50 MB has an RSS of about 50 MB.

definition: Which phase of its life a process is in: in the textbook model new, ready, running, blocked or terminated; in Linux letters such as R, S, D, T and Z.
example: A process waiting for a disk read is in the blocked state.

definition: The state of a process that could run but is waiting for a CPU. Preemption moves a running process back to ready.
example: When its time slice ends, a running process moves to ready.

definition: The state of a process whose thread is executing on a CPU right now. At most one thread runs per logical CPU at any instant.
example: On a 4-core machine without SMT at most 4 threads are in the running state at once.

definition: The state of a process that cannot continue until something happens, such as I/O completing, a lock being released or a timer expiring. A blocked process uses no CPU.
example: A process reading from an empty socket is blocked until data arrives.

definition: The state of a process that has finished running but has not yet been fully cleaned up. On Unix this is a zombie until its parent waits for it.
example: After exit(0), a process is terminated but stays a zombie until reaped.

definition: A process that has exited but whose parent has not yet collected its exit status with wait. It uses no CPU and has no address space, but keeps its PID and a small kernel record.
example: Thousands of <defunct> entries in ps mean a parent is not reaping its children.

definition: A process whose parent has died. The kernel re-parents it to PID 1 or the nearest subreaper, which must reap it when it exits.
example: If a shell dies while a background job runs, the job becomes an orphan adopted by systemd.

definition: A smoothed count of how many tasks were recently running, runnable or (on Linux) in uninterruptible sleep, reported over 1, 5 and 15 minutes. Compare it with the number of logical CPUs.
example: A load average of 8 on an 8-core server means, roughly, every core has had one task wanting it.

definition: A Linux sleep state, shown as D, in which a task waits inside the kernel (usually for I/O) and is not woken by ordinary signals. Linux counts these tasks in the load average.
example: Processes reading from a hung NFS server sit in D state and cannot be killed until the I/O finishes.

definition: A Linux sleep state, shown as S, in which a task waits for an event and can be woken early by a signal.
example: A shell waiting for you to type is in S state.

definition: Keeping several programs in memory at once so that when one waits for I/O, the CPU can run another.
example: While one process waits 5 ms for a disk, another can use the CPU.

definition: The kernel's cache of file contents in otherwise unused RAM. Reads that hit it need no disk I/O.
example: Reading the same file twice is fast the second time because it is in the page cache.

definition: Writing past the end of a buffer, overwriting neighbouring memory. On the stack it can overwrite a return address and let an attacker redirect execution.
example: Copying 200 bytes into a 64-byte stack array is a buffer overflow.

definition: The address a function jumps back to when it finishes, saved on the stack when it was called. Overwriting it is a classic exploit technique.
example: A stack buffer overflow can replace the return address with an attacker-chosen one.

definition: Small pieces of machine code an attacker injects and tries to run, traditionally to start a shell. W^X prevents injected data from being executed directly.
example: Classic exploits wrote shellcode onto the stack and jumped to it.

definition: An exploit technique that chains short snippets of existing code (gadgets), each ending in a return, to perform an attack without injecting new code. It needs to know where those snippets are, which ASLR hides.
example: A ROP chain can call libc functions using gadgets already in memory.

definition: A secret value placed between a function's local buffers and its return address, checked before returning. A buffer overflow that overwrites it is detected and the program aborts.
example: GCC's -fstack-protector inserts stack canaries.

definition: A memory protection policy in which a page may be writable or executable but never both at once, so data an attacker writes cannot be run as code.
example: Text pages are read and execute only; the stack and heap are read and write only.

definition: A bug that reveals memory contents, such as a pointer, to an attacker. One leaked address can defeat ASLR for the whole region it belongs to.
example: Leaking one libc function's address reveals libc's base address.

definition: The standard file format for executables, shared libraries and object files on Linux and most Unix systems. It describes the program's segments (text, data, BSS sizes) for the loader.
example: size ./prog reads the ELF headers and prints the text, data and bss sizes.

definition: The kernel and dynamic-loader code that sets up a program's memory at exec time: mapping its segments, BSS and shared libraries. The linker is the build tool that combined object files into the executable and chose its layout.
example: The loader maps zero-filled pages for BSS rather than reading them from the file.

definition: A compiler optimisation that reuses the current stack frame when a function's last action is to call another function, so deep recursion of that form uses constant stack.
example: Without tail-call elimination, a 100,000-deep recursive function needs 100,000 stack frames.

definition: The glibc implementation of POSIX threads on Linux, in which each thread is a separate kernel task (1:1 threading).
example: Under NPTL, a program with 10 pthreads has 10 kernel tasks.

definition: The standard POSIX API for creating and managing threads in C (pthread_create, pthread_join, mutexes and so on).
example: pthread_attr_setstacksize sets the stack size for a new thread.

definition: The Linux kernel mechanism that, when memory is exhausted, picks a process and kills it with SIGKILL to free memory.
example: A container that exceeds its memory limit is often killed by the OOM killer, showing status 137.

definition: A single physical page full of zeros that Linux can map read-only wherever a program reads memory it has never written. A real private page is only allocated on the first write.
example: Reading a fresh 200 MiB BSS array uses almost no RAM because reads map the zero page.

definition: A memory page much larger than the 4 KiB default (2 MiB or 1 GiB on x86-64), which needs fewer TLB entries. Transparent huge pages (THP) are used automatically by Linux, which can make copy-on-write copy 2 MiB at a time.
example: Redis recommends disabling transparent huge pages because they can worsen fork latency.

definition: Memory not backed by any file, such as the heap, stack and BSS. It starts zero-filled and, if paged out, goes to swap.
example: mmap with MAP_ANONYMOUS creates anonymous memory.

definition: Free memory being scattered in small pieces between allocations still in use, so it cannot be returned to the kernel or used for large requests.
example: One live 100-byte block in a 4 KiB page stops the allocator returning that page.

definition: malloc_trim asks glibc to return free memory to the kernel; madvise is the system call it can use to tell the kernel a range of pages is no longer needed.
example: A long-running service can call malloc_trim(0) after a burst to lower its RSS.

definition: A Unix command that lists processes with their PIDs, states and resource use.
example: ps -o pid,stat,cmd shows each process's state letter, such as Z for zombie.

definition: A Linux tool that shows a live, regularly refreshed list of processes, their states and CPU and memory use, plus the load average.
example: Many processes in state D with idle CPUs in top suggests stuck I/O.

definition: A Linux tool (from the sysstat package) that reports disk I/O statistics, including how busy each device is.
example: iostat -x 1 shows each disk's utilisation every second.

definition: A file holding a snapshot of a crashed process's memory and registers, written for later debugging. It is the default action for signals such as SIGSEGV.
example: Loading a core dump into gdb shows where a program crashed.

definition: Terminal key combinations: Ctrl-C sends SIGINT to the foreground job (usually terminating it) and Ctrl-Z sends SIGTSTP (stopping it).
example: Pressing Ctrl-C on a running command makes Bash report status 130.

definition: The identity information the kernel keeps for a process (user IDs, group IDs, capabilities) and checks on every permission decision.
example: A setuid program runs with its file owner's credentials.

definition: The set of signals a thread has blocked. A blocked signal is not lost: it stays pending until unblocked.
example: Blocking SIGINT during a critical update delays Ctrl-C until the update is done.

definition: A popular high-level programming language. Its interpreter, python3, is an ordinary program that runs as a process.
example: Running python3 three times gives three processes of one program.

definition: The Unix system call that creates a new process (the child) as an almost exact copy of the caller (the parent). It returns twice: the child's PID in the parent and 0 in the child, or -1 on failure.
example: pid_t pid = fork(); if (pid == 0) { /* child */ } else { /* parent */ }

definition: The family of calls that replace the program running in the current process with a new one, keeping the same PID and (unless close-on-exec) open file descriptors. All are wrappers around the execve system call; on success they never return.
example: execvp("ls", argv) turns a forked child into the ls program.

definition: System calls a parent uses to wait for a child to change state (usually exit) and collect its exit status, which also removes the zombie.
example: waitpid(pid, &status, 0) blocks until that child exits.

definition: A process created by another process (its parent), for example with fork. It inherits copies of much of the parent's state.
example: When your shell runs ls, ls is a child process of the shell.

definition: The process that created another process. It is responsible for collecting its children's exit statuses with wait.
example: systemd is the parent of most service processes.

definition: A Linux command that draws the running processes as a family tree.
example: pstree -p shows each process with its PID under its parent.

definition: Sharing memory pages between processes until one of them writes, at which point the kernel gives the writer its own private copy. It makes fork cheap, because pages are only copied if and when they change.
example: After fork, parent and child share every page; the first write by either triggers a fault and a copy of just that page.

definition: The kernel object behind an open file, holding the file offset and status flags. Several file descriptors, even in different processes after fork, can point to the same one and so share its offset.
example: A parent and child that both write to an inherited fd append in turn because they share one open file description.

definition: The position in an open file where the next read or write will happen. It belongs to the open file description, so processes sharing one share the offset.
example: After reading 100 bytes, the file offset is 100.

definition: A lock on a byte range of a file. Classic POSIX record locks taken with fcntl belong to the process and are not inherited by fork; open-file-description locks belong to the open file and are.
example: A database can lock bytes 0–99 of a file with fcntl so another process waits.

definition: Named string settings, such as PATH and HOME, passed to every program a process starts. PATH lists the directories searched for commands.
example: execvp searches each directory in PATH for the program name.

definition: The directory relative file names are resolved from for a process. It is inherited across fork and exec and changed with chdir.
example: After chdir("/tmp"), open("x") opens /tmp/x.

definition: mmap flags. With MAP_SHARED, writes are visible to every process mapping the same object; with MAP_PRIVATE, each process gets copy-on-write private pages.
example: A shared counter between processes needs a MAP_SHARED mapping.

definition: The Redis command that saves a snapshot of the dataset to disk in the background, by forking a child that writes the copy-on-write view while the parent keeps serving.
example: A heavily written Redis can nearly double its memory during BGSAVE.

term: Transparent huge pages and fork latency
definition: Redis documentation warns that transparent huge pages make each copy-on-write fault copy a large page, which can increase fork-related latency and memory use.
example: Redis logs a warning at start-up if transparent huge pages are enabled.

definition: A flag on a file descriptor that makes exec close it automatically, so it does not leak into the new program.
example: open("log", O_WRONLY | O_CLOEXEC) keeps the log fd out of any program the process later execs.

definition: A file permission bit that makes an executable run with its owner's user ID rather than the caller's, and the related system call for changing user ID.
example: passwd is setuid root so it can update the password database.

definition: What a process does when a given signal arrives: the default action (terminate, ignore, stop, core dump), ignore it, or run a handler.
example: SIGCHLD's default disposition is to ignore it.

definition: Special values for a signal disposition: SIG_IGN means ignore the signal, SIG_DFL means use its default action. Ignored dispositions survive exec; handlers do not.
example: signal(SIGPIPE, SIG_IGN) makes writes to a closed pipe fail with EPIPE instead of killing the process.

definition: The system call that makes one file descriptor number refer to the same open file as another, closing whatever it pointed to before. Shells use it for redirection.
example: dup2(fd, 1) makes standard output go wherever fd points.

definition: A shell feature that connects a program's standard input or output to a file instead of the terminal, set up between fork and exec.
example: ls > out.txt redirects the output of ls into out.txt.

definition: A chain of commands connected by pipes, each one's standard output feeding the next one's standard input.
example: ls | wc -l is a two-command pipeline that counts files.

definition: A process group is a set of processes, such as a shell job, that can be signalled together; setpgid moves a process into one.
example: Ctrl-C sends SIGINT to every process in the foreground process group.

definition: A POSIX call that creates a child process and execs a program in one step. glibc (since 2.24) implements it with a clone that shares the parent's memory until exec, avoiding fork's page-table copying.
example: A large Java service can launch a helper with posix_spawn far more cheaply than fork plus exec.

definition: A variant of fork in which the child borrows the parent's memory and the parent is suspended until the child calls exec or _exit. It is fast but easy to misuse.
example: Modifying a variable in a vfork child also changes it in the parent, which is why its use is restricted.

definition: Linux's general process- and thread-creation system call. Flags choose what the new task shares with its creator (memory, files, signal handlers); fork, threads and containers are all clone with different flags.
example: pthread_create calls clone with CLONE_VM so the new thread shares the address space.

definition: The small number a process returns when it ends, 0 for success by convention and anything else for failure. Only the low 8 bits (0–255) reach the parent.
example: exit(2) gives an exit status of 2, which Bash shows in $?.

definition: C macros that decode the status from wait: WIFEXITED says whether the child exited normally and WEXITSTATUS gives its exit code; WIFSIGNALED says whether a signal killed it and WTERMSIG gives which.
example: If WIFSIGNALED(status) is true and WTERMSIG(status) is 9, the child was killed by SIGKILL.

definition: exit() ends a process after running atexit handlers and flushing stdio buffers; _exit() ends it immediately without either. A forked child that fails to exec should use _exit.
example: A failed exec followed by exit() could flush a copy of the parent's buffered output a second time.

definition: A waitpid flag that makes it return immediately (with 0) if no child has exited yet, instead of blocking. It is used in reaping loops.
example: while (waitpid(-1, NULL, WNOHANG) > 0) reaps every child that has exited.

definition: Collecting a dead child's exit status with wait, which lets the kernel free its PID and remaining record. An unreaped child stays a zombie.
example: A SIGCHLD handler that loops on waitpid reaps every exited child.

definition: A process that has asked (with prctl PR_SET_CHILD_SUBREAPER, Linux 3.4 and later) to adopt orphaned descendants instead of PID 1, and so must reap them.
example: systemd's per-user manager is a subreaper for processes in the user session.
