definition: A Linux system call for setting various per-process options, such as becoming a child subreaper.
example: prctl(PR_SET_CHILD_SUBREAPER, 1) makes the caller adopt its orphaned descendants.

definition: A Linux feature giving a group of processes their own PID numbering, starting from 1. Containers use it, so the container's first process is PID 1 inside but has a different PID outside.
example: A container's app sees itself as PID 1, while the host sees it as PID 48213.

definition: A popular tool for building and running containers. docker stop sends the container's main process SIGTERM, waits a grace period (10 seconds by default) and then sends SIGKILL.
example: docker run --init starts a tiny init (tini) as PID 1 in the container.

definition: Tiny init programs designed to run as PID 1 in a container: they forward signals to the application and reap orphaned zombies. docker run --init uses tini.
example: Using tini as the entrypoint stops zombies piling up in a container.

definition: A period allowed before something is acted on. On container platforms it is the time waited after SIGTERM for a process to shut down cleanly before killing it with SIGKILL: 10 seconds by default in Docker, 30 seconds in Kubernetes.
example: A service that finishes in-flight requests within the grace period shuts down without errors.

definition: A system for running and managing containers across a cluster of machines. When it stops a pod it sends SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after a grace period (30 seconds by default).
example: Kubernetes restarts a container whose process exits unexpectedly.

definition: Describes functions that can safely be called from a signal handler (or in a child after a multithreaded fork) because they do not depend on locks or state the interrupted code might hold. write, _exit and kill are; printf and malloc are not.
example: A SIGTERM handler should set a flag or call write, not printf.

definition: Linux's policy of letting processes reserve more memory than is physically available, on the bet that not all of it will be used. vm.overcommit_memory sets how strict it is (0 heuristic, 1 always allow, 2 strict).
example: With vm.overcommit_memory=1, fork of a huge process succeeds, but the OOM killer may strike later.

definition: One entry in a page table, mapping one virtual page to a physical frame with its permission bits. On x86-64 each entry is 8 bytes.
example: Mapping 30 GiB with 4 KiB pages takes 7,864,320 leaf PTEs, about 60 MiB.

definition: A widely used programming language that runs on the Java Virtual Machine (JVM). Large Java services often have big heaps and many threads, which makes fork expensive.
example: A 30 GB Java service should launch helpers with posix_spawn rather than fork.

definition: A JavaScript runtime that handles many connections with a single-threaded event loop and non-blocking I/O.
example: A Node.js server can hold thousands of idle connections on one thread.

definition: Having more than one thread. Forking a multithreaded process is risky because only the calling thread exists in the child, and locks other threads held stay locked.
example: A web server with 64 worker threads is a multithreaded process.

definition: A synchronisation object that controls access to shared data. In the simplest kind (a mutual-exclusion lock, or mutex) only one thread or process can hold it at a time; a read-write lock allows one writer or many readers. A thread wanting a held lock waits, by blocking or spinning.
example: If a thread holding malloc's lock vanishes after fork, malloc in the child can wait for ever.

definition: A context switch that happens because the running task cannot continue, for example it blocked on I/O, a lock or sleep, and gave up the CPU.
example: A thread calling read on an empty socket makes a voluntary context switch.

definition: A context switch where the kernel takes the CPU from a task that could have kept running, because its time slice ended or a higher-priority task woke (preemption).
example: A CPU-bound loop racks up involuntary context switches.

definition: Waiting inside the kernel, off the CPU, until something happens, such as data arriving or a lock being released. A blocking call does not return until then.
example: A blocking read on an empty pipe sleeps until a writer adds data.

definition: Not waiting: a non-blocking operation returns straight away instead of making its caller wait. For I/O it means calls that return immediately (with EAGAIN) when no data or space is available, so one thread can juggle many connections with epoll or io_uring.
example: An nginx worker uses non-blocking sockets and epoll to serve thousands of clients.

definition: A thread switch changes which thread runs but keeps the address space; a process switch also changes the address space (page tables), so it can cost more.
example: Switching between two threads of one server is a thread switch; switching to a different program is a process switch.

definition: The x86 control register that holds the physical address of the current page-table root. Writing a new value switches address spaces, which without PCID also flushes non-global TLB entries.
example: switch_mm loads the next process's page-table root into CR3.

definition: The top-level page table of a process, from which the MMU walks down to translate any address. Loading a different root switches to a different address space.
example: On x86 the page-table root's address lives in CR3.

definition: A register that a function must preserve for its caller. When switching kernel stacks, Linux only needs to save these explicitly; the rest were saved on kernel entry.
example: On x86-64, rbx, rbp and r12 to r15 are callee-saved.

definition: The part of the CPU that does floating-point arithmetic, with its own registers. Its state, together with SIMD registers, must be saved and restored on a context switch.
example: A program doing double arithmetic uses FPU and SSE registers.

definition: x86 SIMD instruction-set extensions with wide registers (128-bit for SSE, 256-bit for AVX, 512-bit for AVX-512). AVX-512 state is over 2 KiB, which makes saving it on a switch costly.
example: Video encoders use AVX instructions to process many pixels per instruction.

definition: x86 instructions that save and restore extended CPU state (FPU, SSE, AVX) in one go, skipping components that have not been used.
example: The kernel uses XSAVE to store a task's AVX registers when switching it out.

definition: Variables that have a separate copy for each thread, such as errno. On x86-64 Linux the FS register points to the current thread's block, so it must be switched with the thread.
example: Each thread's errno is a thread-local variable.

definition: An x86-64 segment register whose base address Linux uses to point at the current thread's thread-local storage.
example: Switching threads changes the FS base so errno refers to the new thread's copy.

definition: A small stack (typically 16 KiB on x86-64) that each task uses while running kernel code. Its user registers are pushed there on kernel entry, so switching tasks is mostly swapping kernel stacks.
example: switch_to saves the old task's kernel stack pointer and loads the new one's.

definition: A Linux command that sets which CPUs a process may run on (its CPU affinity).
example: taskset -c 0 ./pp runs pp only on CPU 0.

definition: Which CPUs a task is allowed, or prefers, to run on. Pinning a task to one CPU keeps its cache warm and avoids migrations; Linux also prefers to keep tasks where they last ran (cache affinity).
example: Pinning both ping-pong processes to CPU 0 measures true same-core switches.

definition: A suite of operating-system micro-benchmarks. Its lat_ctx tool measures context-switch time by passing a token between processes through pipes.
example: lat_ctx -s 0 2 measures switching between two processes with tiny working sets.

definition: The memory a task actively uses over a short period. If it fits in the caches the task runs fast; another task running in between can evict it.
example: A 512 KiB working set is 8,192 cache lines of 64 bytes.

definition: The fixed-size block of memory (64 bytes on typical x86-64 CPUs) that caches store and move as a unit.
example: Reading one byte brings the whole 64-byte cache line into the cache.

definition: When requested data is not in a cache, so it must be fetched from a slower level or RAM. A TLB miss is the same idea for address translations.
example: After a switch, a task's first accesses often miss in the cache.

definition: A CPU's ability to have several cache misses outstanding at once, so their latencies overlap instead of adding up.
example: With 10 misses in flight, refilling 8,192 lines takes far less than 8,192 times one miss latency.

definition: The MMU reading down the levels of the page tables to translate an address after a TLB miss: several dependent memory reads.
example: With four-level paging a TLB miss can need four memory reads before the real access.

definition: Discarding cached address translations from the TLB, so following accesses miss and need page-table walks.
example: Writing CR3 without PCID flushes the TLB of the old process's translations.

definition: A page marked so its TLB entry survives address-space switches, used for mappings that are the same in every process, such as parts of the kernel.
example: Writing CR3 keeps global entries but flushes non-global ones.

definition: An x86 feature that tags TLB entries with an address-space ID, so translations for several address spaces (and for KPTI's user and kernel tables) can coexist and survive CR3 writes. Linux uses it since 4.14.
example: With PCID, a syscall under KPTI does not have to start with an empty TLB.

definition: A tag on TLB entries identifying which address space they belong to, letting entries from several processes coexist. ARM's ASID plays the same role as x86's PCID.
example: Switching back to a recent process on ARM can reuse its TLB entries thanks to ASIDs.

definition: Telling other CPUs, usually with an inter-processor interrupt, to discard TLB entries for a mapping that has changed.
example: Unmapping memory in a multithreaded process can trigger TLB shootdowns on every core running its threads.

definition: A cache is cold for a task when little of its data is in it, so accesses miss; warm when its data is already there. Switching tasks tends to leave caches cold for the newcomer.
example: A task resumed after a long gap runs slowly at first on a cold cache.

definition: Moving a task to run on a different CPU core, which can lose the data it had in that core's private caches.
example: perf stat -e cpu-migrations counts how often tasks moved between cores.

definition: The hardware protocol that keeps each core's cached copy of the same memory consistent. Moving data between cores this way costs time.
example: Two processes on different cores writing one shared counter bounce its cache line back and forth.

definition: A Linux tool that reports system-wide statistics each interval, including context switches per second in its cs column.
example: vmstat 1 prints one line of statistics every second.

definition: A Linux tool (sysstat package) that reports per-task statistics; -w shows voluntary and involuntary context switches per second.
example: pidstat -w 1 shows which processes are switching most.

definition: The Linux performance-analysis tool. perf stat counts events such as context switches, migrations and cache misses; perf sched records scheduler activity and latency.
example: perf stat -e context-switches,cpu-migrations ./prog counts both for one run.

definition: A server design that gives each client connection its own thread. Simple, but with many busy connections the threads compete for the cores.
example: A thread-per-connection server with 10,000 busy clients on 16 cores has about 625 runnable threads per core.

definition: A fixed set of worker threads that take tasks from a queue, instead of creating a thread per task. Keeping it near the number of cores limits switching.
example: A server with 16 cores might run a pool of 16 worker threads.

definition: A Linux interface that lets one thread wait efficiently on many file descriptors at once and learn which are ready.
example: An event loop calls epoll_wait to find which of 10,000 sockets have data.

definition: A program structure in which one thread repeatedly waits for ready events (such as from epoll) and handles each quickly without blocking.
example: Node.js and nginx workers run event loops.

definition: Competition between threads for the same shared resource at once, most often a lock (but also a CPU or a cache line). With lock contention most of the threads wait; waiting threads may block and cause extra context switches.
example: Sharding one hot lock into 16 reduces lock contention.

definition: A stretch of code that accesses shared data and so must be run by only one thread at a time, usually by holding a lock.
example: Keeping critical sections short means locks are held briefly.

definition: Splitting one lock into several, each protecting part of the data, so threads touching different parts do not contend.
example: A hash table with one lock per bucket group shards its lock.

definition: A mutex that spins (repeatedly checks) for a short time before sleeping, betting the holder will release it soon, because a short spin is cheaper than two context switches.
example: Linux kernel mutexes spin while the lock owner is running on another CPU.

definition: A set of libraries for very fast packet processing in user space, bypassing the kernel network stack and busy-polling network cards on dedicated cores.
example: A DPDK packet processor dedicates whole cores to polling NICs.

definition: A Linux boot parameter that removes chosen CPUs from normal scheduling, so only tasks explicitly placed there run on them.
example: isolcpus=2,3 keeps ordinary tasks off CPUs 2 and 3 for a latency-critical app.

definition: Repeatedly checking for new work in a tight loop instead of sleeping and being woken, trading CPU time for lower latency.
example: A trading system busy-polls its network card so it reacts within microseconds.

definition: A thread managed by a runtime library in user space rather than by the kernel. Switching between them needs no kernel entry, but a blocking syscall blocks the kernel thread underneath.
example: Go goroutines are user-level threads scheduled by the Go runtime.

definition: Ways to map user threads onto kernel threads. 1:1 gives each user thread its own kernel thread; N:1 runs N user threads on one kernel thread; M:N runs M user threads over a pool of N kernel threads. The first number counts user threads.
example: Linux pthreads are 1:1; Go goroutines are M:N.

definition: A lightweight thread in the Go programming language, scheduled by the Go runtime onto a smaller number of OS threads (M:N threading). Each starts with a small stack (2 KiB in current Go releases) that the runtime grows as needed.
example: A Go server can run 100,000 goroutines on a handful of OS threads.

term: Java virtual threads and platform threads
definition: Java platform threads map 1:1 to OS threads; virtual threads (standard since JDK 21) are lightweight threads the JVM schedules M:N onto a pool of platform threads.
example: A Java server can create a virtual thread per request without exhausting OS threads.

definition: An interrupt one CPU core sends to another, for example to wake it to run a task or to make it flush TLB entries.
example: Waking a task that sleeps on another core may need an IPI.

definition: A power-saving mode an idle CPU core drops into. Waking from a deeper idle state takes longer, adding to wake-up latency.
example: A core in a deep idle state can take tens of microseconds to wake.

definition: Having more runnable threads than cores, so they must take turns and switch frequently.
example: 10,000 busy threads on 16 cores is heavy oversubscription.

definition: The scheduler's per-CPU collection of runnable tasks waiting for that CPU.
example: A long run queue means tasks wait longer before getting a turn.

definition: A CPU-bound task spends its time computing and would use more CPU if given it; an I/O-bound task spends most of its time waiting for I/O.
example: Video encoding is CPU-bound; a chat server is usually I/O-bound.

definition: CPU time spent running kernel code on behalf of processes, as opposed to user time spent in their own code. High system time often means many syscalls or context switches.
example: top shows system time as "sy" in its CPU line.

definition: A measurement in which two processes pass a byte back and forth through a pair of pipes many times, to estimate switch and wake-up cost from the total time.
example: 100,000 round trips in 0.5 s means 5 µs per round trip.

definition: A one-way kernel buffer with two file descriptors: one end for writing and one for reading. Bytes come out in the order they went in; reads block when it is empty and writes block when it is full.
example: pipe(fd) puts the read end in fd[0] and the write end in fd[1].

definition: How many bytes a pipe can hold before writers block: 65,536 bytes (16 pages of 4 KiB) by default on Linux, queryable with F_GETPIPE_SZ and changeable with F_SETPIPE_SZ up to /proc/sys/fs/pipe-max-size.
example: A writer of 4,096-byte chunks fills a default Linux pipe after 16 writes.

definition: The largest pipe write guaranteed to be atomic, meaning it will not be interleaved with other writers' data: 4,096 bytes on Linux; POSIX requires at least 512.
example: Log lines under 4,096 bytes from many processes arrive in one pipe unbroken.

definition: A write that happens all at once from the reader's point of view, with no other writer's data mixed into it.
example: A 200-byte pipe write is atomic on Linux; a 10 KiB write may not be.

definition: The marker of where one message ends and the next begins. Pipes and stream sockets do not keep them; message queues and datagram sockets do.
example: Two 5-byte writes to a pipe can be read back as one 10-byte chunk, because the boundary is lost.

definition: A channel that delivers an ordered sequence of bytes with no built-in division into messages, such as a pipe or TCP connection.
example: A byte stream can deliver two writes of 10 bytes as reads of 7 and 13 bytes.

term: FIFO (first in, first out; named pipe)
definition: First in, first out: items leave in the order they arrived, as in a queue or a pipe; as a policy (FIFO scheduling, FIFO page replacement) it means serving or evicting the oldest first. In Unix, "a FIFO" also means a named pipe: a pipe with a name in the file system, created with mkfifo, so unrelated processes can open it. Its data still passes through a kernel buffer, not the disk.
example: mkfifo /tmp/jobs creates a FIFO that one process writes and another reads, byte for byte in order.

definition: A small numbered notification the kernel delivers to a process asynchronously to say something happened, such as Ctrl-C or a child exiting. The process can take the default action, ignore it, block it or run a handler.
example: kill -TERM 1234 sends signal 15 to process 1234.

definition: The interrupt signal (2 on Linux), sent by Ctrl-C. Its default action terminates the process.
example: Pressing Ctrl-C sends SIGINT to the foreground job.

definition: The polite termination signal (15 on Linux), sent by kill and by container platforms at shutdown. Programs can catch it to clean up.
example: docker stop sends SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after 10 seconds.

definition: The signal (9 on Linux) that terminates a process without any chance to clean up. It cannot be caught, blocked or ignored.
example: kill -9 1234 sends SIGKILL; Bash then reports status 137.

definition: The signal (19 on x86 and ARM Linux) that stops (pauses) a process; it cannot be caught, blocked or ignored. SIGCONT resumes it, and SIGTSTP is the catchable stop sent by Ctrl-Z.
example: kill -STOP 1234 freezes a process until kill -CONT 1234.

definition: The signal (13 on Linux) sent to a process that writes to a pipe or socket with no reader left. By default it terminates the writer.
example: In yes | head -n 1, yes dies from SIGPIPE when head exits.

definition: The signal (17 on x86 and ARM Linux) sent to a parent when a child exits or stops. It is ignored by default; setting it explicitly to SIG_IGN makes Linux reap children automatically.
example: A server can reap children in a SIGCHLD handler with a WNOHANG loop.

definition: The hangup signal (1), originally sent when a terminal disconnected. Many daemons treat it as "reload your configuration".
example: kill -HUP on nginx's master process makes it reload its config.

definition: Signals with no predefined meaning, left for applications to use as they choose.
example: Some programs reopen their log files on SIGUSR1.

definition: Linux signals numbered from SIGRTMIN to SIGRTMAX that, unlike standard signals, queue: each one sent is delivered separately, in order.
example: Sending SIGRTMIN three times delivers it three times, whereas three SIGCHLDs may arrive as one.

definition: A sigaction flag that makes the kernel pass the handler extra information about the signal, such as the sender's PID.
example: With SA_SIGINFO, a SIGCHLD handler can see which child exited.

definition: A C integer type that can be read and written in one indivisible step even if a signal arrives, used (as volatile sig_atomic_t) for flags a handler sets.
example: static volatile sig_atomic_t stop; is set to 1 by a SIGTERM handler.

definition: A C keyword telling the compiler a variable may change outside the normal flow of the code, so every access must really read or write memory.
example: Without volatile, a loop checking a signal flag could be optimised into an infinite loop.

definition: A Linux system call that turns selected signals into readable events on a file descriptor, so they can be handled in an ordinary event loop instead of a handler.
example: A server adds a signalfd to its epoll set to receive SIGTERM as a normal event.

definition: The command and system call that send a signal to a process, SIGTERM by default.
example: kill 1234 sends SIGTERM to process 1234.

definition: Memory that more than one process or thread can read and write directly. In an operating system it usually means memory mapped into two or more processes' address spaces so they share data without copying it through the kernel. It needs separate synchronisation and notification.
example: PostgreSQL backend processes share their buffer cache through shared memory.

definition: POSIX calls to create (or open) and remove a named shared memory object. On Linux these objects live in the tmpfs at /dev/shm and persist until unlinked or reboot.
example: shm_open("/stats", O_CREAT | O_RDWR, 0600) creates /dev/shm/stats.

definition: The system call that sets the size of an open file or shared memory object.
example: ftruncate(fd, 4096) makes a new shared memory object 4,096 bytes long.

definition: A mutex or semaphore placed in shared memory and marked so threads in different processes can use it to coordinate.
example: Two processes updating one shared counter can protect it with a process-shared mutex.

definition: A Linux "fast user-space mutex" system call: threads wait on and wake each other through an integer in shared memory, entering the kernel only when they must sleep or wake someone.
example: glibc's mutexes are built on futexes.

definition: A named kernel object that holds discrete messages with priorities. mq_receive returns the oldest highest-priority message. On Linux the defaults allow 10 messages of up to 8 KiB.
example: mq_send(q, "resize img7", 12, 5) queues a 12-byte message at priority 5.

definition: An older family of Unix IPC interfaces (message queues, semaphores, shared memory) using numeric keys. It still works but is awkward compared with the POSIX equivalents.
example: msgget and msgsnd are the System V message-queue calls.

definition: Slowing a fast producer down to a slow consumer's pace, usually by making it block or fail when a bounded buffer is full.
example: A full pipe blocks the writer, which is back-pressure.

definition: A socket for communication between processes on the same machine, addressed by a file path or abstract name. It is bidirectional, supports streams and messages, can pass file descriptors and can report the peer's credentials.
example: Docker's command-line tool talks to the daemon over /var/run/docker.sock, a Unix domain socket.

definition: SOCK_STREAM is a reliable byte stream; SOCK_DGRAM sends separate datagrams (reliable and ordered on Unix sockets); SOCK_SEQPACKET sends messages in order with boundaries over a connection.
example: A logger can use a SOCK_DGRAM Unix socket so each record arrives whole.

definition: A self-contained message sent as one unit, received whole or not at all.
example: Each sendto on a SOCK_DGRAM socket sends one datagram.

definition: Socket calls: a client calls connect to reach a listening server, and the server calls accept to get a new socket for that connection.
example: A database server accepts each client connection on its Unix socket.

definition: Socket system calls that send and receive a message together with ancillary (control) data, such as file descriptors.
example: sendmsg with an SCM_RIGHTS control message passes an fd to another process.

definition: A control message on a Unix domain socket that carries open file descriptors. The kernel installs new descriptors in the receiver that refer to the same open files.
example: A privileged daemon can accept a TCP connection and hand the socket to a sandboxed worker with SCM_RIGHTS.

definition: A Unix-socket option that reports the PID, UID and GID of the process at the other end, as verified by the kernel.
example: PostgreSQL's peer authentication uses it to check the connecting OS user.

definition: A Linux display protocol in which applications (clients) send drawing buffers to a compositor, the program that combines them on screen, passing buffer fds over a Unix socket.
example: A Wayland client shares its window buffer with the compositor by fd passing.

definition: Splitting a program into a small privileged part and less-privileged (sandboxed) parts that do most of the work, so a bug in the latter does less damage.
example: OpenSSH uses privilege separation so network parsing happens in an unprivileged process.

definition: A message bus for Linux desktop and system services, running over Unix domain sockets.
example: NetworkManager and desktop apps talk to each other over D-Bus.

definition: Android's IPC system, implemented as its own Linux kernel driver, through which apps and system services call each other.
example: An Android app reaches the camera service via Binder.

definition: Google's mobile operating system, built on the Linux kernel.
example: Android apps run as separate Linux processes with separate user IDs.

definition: The virtual network interface (127.0.0.1) that connects a machine to itself. TCP over loopback still runs the full TCP/IP stack.
example: Connecting to localhost:5432 uses loopback TCP; connecting via /var/run/postgresql uses a Unix socket.

definition: A small value computed from data to detect corruption. TCP/IP computes them on every packet; Unix sockets skip them.
example: A TCP segment carries a 16-bit checksum.

definition: TCP's mechanism for slowing down when the network seems overloaded. It is unnecessary between processes on one machine.
example: TCP congestion control halves its sending window after detecting loss.

definition: A widely used open-source relational database. Its clients use a Unix socket by default for local "localhost" connections on Unix systems.
example: mysql -u root with no host connects over the Unix socket.

definition: In PostgreSQL, the separate server process that handles one client connection; backends share data through shared memory.
example: A PostgreSQL server with 100 connections runs 100 backend processes.

definition: Moving data without copying it between buffers, for example by remapping pages or letting the kernel send directly from the page cache.
example: sendfile is a zero-copy way to send a file to a socket.

definition: A Linux system call (5.6 and later) that copies a file descriptor from another process, given suitable permission.
example: A debugger could use pidfd_getfd to inspect a target process's open socket.

definition: A send flag that stops a write to a broken connection raising SIGPIPE; the call fails with EPIPE instead.
example: send(fd, buf, n, MSG_NOSIGNAL) cannot kill a server that forgot to ignore SIGPIPE.

definition: Removing a name from the file system (or from /dev/shm). The object itself goes away once nothing uses it.
example: Calling unlink on a FIFO path at startup cleans up after a previous crash.

definition: A Bash array variable holding the exit status of every command in the most recent pipeline.
example: After yes | head -n 1, ${PIPESTATUS[0]} is 141 for yes.

definition: Coordinating threads or processes that share data, with locks, semaphores or atomic operations, so updates are not lost or seen half-done.
example: Two processes incrementing a shared counter need synchronisation or updates can be lost.

definition: When two unsynchronised read-modify-write operations overlap and one overwrites the other's result.
example: Both processes read 5, both add 1, both store 6: one increment is lost.

definition: A position measured from the start of a region. Storing offsets rather than raw pointers in shared memory works even when the region is mapped at different addresses.
example: Store "item at offset 128" rather than the address 0x7f...080.

definition: A request going to the other side and the reply coming back. Between processes on one machine it means a message and its answer, often involving two wake-ups or switches.
example: In the ping-pong benchmark, one round trip is the byte going to the child and coming back.

definition: Memory whose page-table entries forbid writes, such as program code and string literals. A write to it faults.
example: Writing to a string literal on Linux hits a read-only mapping and usually crashes with SIGSEGV.

definition: The kernel code that runs when leaving the kernel to go back to user mode: it delivers pending signals, restores user registers and executes sysret or iret.
example: A pending signal is delivered on the return path of the next syscall.

definition: One of several processes that do the actual work for a server, usually under a parent (master) process that starts and supervises them.
example: nginx runs a master process plus one worker process per core.

definition: The kernel deliberately granting a user-space program access to particular device memory, I/O ports or DMA, for example through UIO or VFIO, so it can act as a driver.
example: A user-space network driver can be given delegated access to one NIC's registers.

definition: The time a process or thread has actually spent running on a CPU, as opposed to waiting. The kernel accounts for it per task and splits it into user time and system time.
example: A process that ran for 10 seconds but spent most of it blocked on disk might have used only 0.2 s of CPU time.

definition: A value the true quantity cannot exceed. A measurement that includes extra work besides the thing you want is an upper bound on that thing's cost.
example: If a round trip with two switches takes 5 µs, each switch costs at most 2.5 µs: an upper bound.

definition: The central loop of a long-running program that repeatedly waits for and handles work. Signal handlers often just set a flag that the main loop checks.
example: while (!stop) do_work(); is a server's main loop.

definition: The basic unit of computer memory and storage: 8 bits, enough for one value from 0 to 255.
example: The text "hi\n" is 3 bytes.

definition: A binary digit, 0 or 1, the smallest unit of information. 8 bits make a byte.
example: An exit status has 8 bits, so it can be 0 to 255.

definition: A unit of 1,024 bytes (2 to the power 10).
example: A 4 KiB page is 4,096 bytes.

definition: A unit of 1,048,576 bytes (1,024 KiB).
example: An 8 MiB stack is 8,192 KiB.

definition: A unit of 1,073,741,824 bytes (1,024 MiB).
example: A 1 GiB file copied in 4 KiB chunks needs 262,144 reads.

definition: A unit of 1,099,511,627,776 bytes (1,024 GiB, or 2 to the power 40).
example: With four-level paging, Linux user space spans 128 TiB.

definition: A unit of 1,024 TiB (2 to the power 50 bytes).
example: Five-level paging gives Linux processes up to 64 PiB of user address space.

definition: A unit of 1,000 bytes in SI usage, though many tools (including /proc on Linux, which writes "kB") mean 1,024 bytes.
example: VmRSS: 1024 kB in /proc means about 1 MiB is resident.

definition: A unit of 1,000,000 bytes (SI). Tools sometimes use MB loosely for 1,048,576 bytes (a MiB).
example: A 100 MB file is 100,000,000 bytes.

definition: A unit of 1,000,000,000 bytes (SI). Memory sizes quoted in GB often really mean GiB.
example: A 20 GB Redis dataset may need about 40 GB during a write-heavy snapshot.

definition: One billionth of a second (0.000000001 s). A cache hit takes about a nanosecond; a syscall often tens to hundreds.
example: 500 ns is half a microsecond.

definition: One millionth of a second, or 1,000 nanoseconds.
example: 5,000 ns is 5 µs.

definition: One thousandth of a second, or 1,000 microseconds.
example: 524,288 syscalls at 500 ns each take about 262 ms.

definition: The SI base unit of time. 1 s = 1,000 ms = 1,000,000 µs = 1,000,000,000 ns.
example: 200 million syscalls at 200 ns each take 40 seconds.

definition: The core of an operating system: the code that runs in kernel mode with full access to the hardware. It creates processes and threads, schedules them, manages memory and devices, and offers its services to programs only through system calls.
example: When a program calls read(), the CPU switches into the kernel, which fetches the data and returns to the program.

definition: A request from a user-mode program to the kernel, made with a special trap instruction (syscall on x86-64, svc on ARM) that switches the CPU into kernel mode at an entry point the kernel chose. It is the only way a program can open files, create processes or use devices.
example: write(1, "hi\n", 3) is a system call: on x86-64 Linux it puts 1 in rax and executes the syscall instruction.

definition: The kernel stopping one task on a CPU and starting another: it saves the old task's registers, switches kernel stacks and, if the new task belongs to a different process, switches page tables. Besides the direct cost, the incoming task often finds the caches and TLB cold.
example: A thread that blocks on a read causes a voluntary context switch to another runnable thread.

definition: One independent sequence of execution inside a process, with its own registers, instruction pointer and stack. Threads of the same process share its address space and open files. On Linux each thread is a separate kernel task that the scheduler runs on its own.
example: A web server process with 64 threads can serve 64 requests at once on a machine with enough cores.

definition: The CPU exception raised when a memory access cannot be completed with the current page-table entry: the page is not mapped yet, or the access breaks its permissions. The kernel then maps a page (for lazy allocation or copy-on-write) and retries, or sends the process SIGSEGV.
example: The first write to a freshly malloc'd page causes a page fault, after which the kernel supplies a zero-filled physical page.

definition: The scheme in which every process uses its own virtual addresses, which the MMU translates through page tables to physical memory. It isolates processes from one another and lets the kernel share, copy-on-write, swap out or lazily allocate pages.
example: Two processes can both use address 0x400000 and see different data, because virtual memory maps each to a different physical frame.

definition: The per-process data structure, kept in memory by the kernel and read by the MMU, that maps each virtual page to a physical frame together with its permission bits. On x86-64 it is a tree of four (or five) levels.
example: Switching to another process means loading the address of its page-table root into CR3.

definition: A small cache inside the CPU of recent virtual-to-physical address translations, so most memory accesses avoid walking the page tables. Switching address spaces can flush it, unless entries are tagged with PCIDs or ASIDs.
example: A TLB hit translates an address almost for free; a miss on x86-64 can cost four extra memory reads for a page-table walk.

definition: A small, fast store that keeps copies of recently used data so later accesses avoid a slower one. In this subject it usually means the CPU caches (L1 to L3) between the cores and RAM; the kernel's page cache does the same job for file data held in RAM.
example: Data in the L1 cache can be read in about a nanosecond; the same data from RAM takes closer to a hundred.

definition: A Linux kernel feature that gives a group of processes its own isolated view of a global resource: PIDs, mounts, network interfaces, hostnames, user IDs and more. Containers are built from namespaces plus cgroups. More generally, a namespace is any set of names in which each name is unique.
example: In a new PID namespace the first process sees itself as PID 1; in a new network namespace it sees only its own interfaces.

definition: The particular sequence of code a program or the kernel runs to handle one kind of operation. A fast path is the common, cheap route; a slow path handles rarer cases at greater cost.
example: clock_gettime normally takes the vDSO fast path; if the clock source cannot be read in user mode it falls back to a real syscall.

definition: Code added to a running kernel to extend it, such as a driver. On macOS these were called kexts and ran in kernel space with full privilege; on Linux the equivalents are loadable kernel modules and, in a checked and restricted form, eBPF programs.
example: Apple now steers USB driver writers from kernel extensions to DriverKit, which runs drivers in user space.
